questions.question: An automated prover is required to find a derivation for every first-order formula that is true in all structures. Which celebrated theorem guarantees such a complete proof calculus exists?
questions.explanation: Gödel's completeness theorem (1930): every semantically valid first-order formula is provable — validity coincides with derivability.

questions.question: A project aims to axiomatize arithmetic so that every truth about the natural numbers becomes provable. Gödel showed any consistent, recursively axiomatized system containing arithmetic leaves some true sentence unprovable. Which theorem establishes this?
questions.explanation: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem: no consistent, effectively axiomatized extension of arithmetic proves every arithmetical truth.

questions.question: An axiomatization intended to capture only the real numbers turns out to have a countable model as well. Which theorem forces every satisfiable first-order theory in a countable language to admit a countable model?
questions.explanation: The downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem says a first-order theory with an infinite model has a countable model — so no first-order theory pins down an uncountable domain.

questions.question: To show an infinite set of constraints has a solution, a logician proves every finite subset is solvable and invokes the theorem that lifts satisfiability from all finite subsets to the whole set. Which theorem does this?
questions.explanation: The compactness theorem: a set of first-order sentences is satisfiable if and only if every finite subset is satisfiable.

questions.question: To ready ∀x∃y L(x,y) for a resolution prover, a preprocessor deletes ∃y and replaces y by a function term f(x) built from the enclosing universal, producing ∀x L(x,f(x)). What is this elimination of existential quantifiers called?
questions.explanation: Skolemization replaces each existentially quantified variable with a function of the enclosing universal variables, preserving satisfiability (not logical equivalence).

questions.question: A first-order prover tests unsatisfiability by generating ground instances of clauses over the language's own terms and checking them propositionally. Which theorem justifies reducing first-order unsatisfiability to finite sets of ground instances?
questions.explanation: Herbrand's theorem: a set of clauses is unsatisfiable iff some finite set of its ground instances is propositionally unsatisfiable, linking first-order to propositional logic.

questions.question: A refutation prover unifies the literal P(x) with P(a), applies the substitution to the clause (¬P(x)∨Q(x)), and derives Q(a). Robinson's complete refutation calculus based on unification is known as what?
questions.explanation: Robinson's resolution principle combines unification with the propositional resolution rule, giving a complete refutation system for first-order clauses.

questions.question: To express 'every nonempty bounded set of reals has a least upper bound' in a single sentence, quantifiers must range over sets of reals, not just individual reals. Which logic is required?
questions.explanation: Second-order logic permits quantification over predicates and sets — forbidden in first-order logic — giving the extra expressive power needed here.

questions.question: A language designer argues no formalism exceeds Turing machines in power, citing the thesis identifying effective computability with λ-calculus or Turing-machine computability. Name this thesis.
questions.explanation: The Church-Turing thesis identifies the intuitive notion of effective computability with what Turing machines — equivalently λ-calculus — can compute.

questions.question: Propositional validity can be settled mechanically: enumerate all 2ⁿ assignments and inspect the column — the procedure always halts with a verdict. Which property of the logic makes this algorithmic check possible?
questions.explanation: A logic is decidable when some algorithm always terminates with the correct yes/no verdict; propositional validity is decidable via truth tables.

questions.question: A startup proposes an algorithm that, given any first-order sentence, always halts and reports whether it is valid. Which theorem shows this project is doomed for full first-order logic?
alternatives: the undecidability theorem for first-order logic
questions.explanation: Church's theorem (1936) proves validity of first-order formulas is undecidable — no general algorithm settles every case.

questions.question: After Skolemizing, a formula reads ∀x₁∀x₂∀x₃ applied to a quantifier-free matrix — a block of universal quantifiers followed by a formula with no quantifiers. What is this shape called?
questions.explanation: Skolem normal form is the ∀-only prenex shape ∀x₁…∀xₙ φ with φ quantifier-free, reached by prenexing and Skolemizing away every ∃.

questions.question: An automated theorem prover interprets a clause set over a domain containing only the language's own ground terms — for a constant a and function f it enumerates {a, f(a), f(f(a)), …}. What is such an interpretation called?
questions.explanation: A Herbrand interpretation/model is built over the Herbrand universe of ground terms; for clause sets, satisfiability can be tested over it.

questions.question: Given φ ⊨ ψ, a verification tool extracts a formula θ using only vocabulary shared by φ and ψ, with φ ⊨ θ and θ ⊨ ψ, to explain the entailment. Which theorem guarantees such an interpolant always exists?
questions.explanation: Craig's interpolation theorem: if φ ⊨ ψ there exists a formula θ over the common language with φ ⊨ θ and θ ⊨ ψ.

questions.question: The theory of real closed fields settles every sentence of its language: for each σ, either the theory proves σ or it proves ¬σ. What is such a theory called?
questions.explanation: A theory is complete when it decides every sentence of its language — proves σ or ¬σ for every σ.

questions.question: Over the domain {2, 4, 6} with P(x,y) meaning x<y, evaluate ∃x∀y P(x,y).
questions.explanation: y ranges over the whole domain including x itself, so x<x refutes the claim for every candidate x.

questions.question: Convert ∀x(P(x)→∃y Q(x,y)) to prenex normal form.
alternatives: forall x exists y (P(x) implies Q(x,y))
questions.explanation: Since y is not free in P(x), P→∃yQ ≡ ∃y(P→Q); the existential pulls out in front.

questions.question: Over the domain {1, 2, 3}, for how many values of x does ∃y(y>x) fail — i.e., how many counterexamples refute ∀x∃y(y>x)?
questions.explanation: x=1 and x=2 each have a greater y in the domain; only x=3 lacks a witness.

questions.question: On the two-element domain {a,b}, expand ∃x∀y L(x,y) into an equivalent quantifier-free formula.
questions.explanation: The outer ∃ becomes a disjunction over {a,b}; each inner ∀ becomes a conjunction over {a,b}.

questions.question: Negate ∀x∃y(P(x)→Q(x,y)) and push the negation fully inward to the predicates.
alternatives: exists x for all y, P(x) and not Q(x,y)
questions.explanation: Quantifier duality flips each quantifier (¬∀→∃¬, ¬∃→∀¬), and ¬(P→Q) = P∧¬Q.
